newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-MPs demand changes to consumer credit plans.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs demand changes to consumer credit plans.

text.p: European Commission plans to give consumers greater protection against abusive credit terms are generally good but need amending, the European Parliament said on Thursday.

Euro-MPs welcomed the main aim of draft directive COM(96)76, which will impose throughout the European Union a uniform method (the AIBD) for calculating the annual percentage rate of charge for credit (APR).
The main effect will be to force Germany, France and Finland to fall into line with the practice already adopted by the other member states.

But parliament said that while the proposal was an improvement on an existing consumer credit directive, 90/88/EEC, and would particularly benefit customers in border areas, the Commission's ideas for calculating the AIBD were flawed.
The Commission recommends the AIBD be set according to a "same-day calculation", whereby the period of a loan is calculated from the first to the last day.

Euro-MPs said a same-day calculation would have a drawback for customers because the level of the APR would depend on the date on which the loan was paid out and could alter from one month to the next, according to the number of days in the month.
Thus an offer made by a credit institution in January, which has 31 days, would be more favourable than a rival offer drawn up in February, which has two or three days fewer.
Instead, Euro-MPs recommended a standardised calculation, based on the subdivision of a year into equal intervals.

Giving the draft directive a first reading (co- decision procedure), Euro-MPs also rejected the Commission's plan to introduce an identical symbol -- a percentage sign surrounded by the 12 EU stars -- indicating that the uniform AIBD is being used to calculate the APR.

Although the idea of a symbol would in theory allow customers to directly compare APR rates, Euro-MPs said this would be misleading at the present time because the member states still worked out APRs in a different way.
"There are so many elements used to define the APR and we only have harmonisation on some points," rapporteur Marlies Mosiek-Urbahn told Reuters last week.
"We will have to wait until there is more harmonisation," the German Christian Democrat said, adding that this would be difficult to achieve in the near future.
Consumer Affairs Commissioner Emma Bonino told parliament on Wednesday the Commission could not accept the parliament's amendment on the calculation method.
The 12 star symbol had been proposed on a request from the member states, Bonino said.
